newsitem.title: USA: Top USDA nutrition policymaker resigns.
newsitem.headline: Top USDA nutrition policymaker resigns.

text.p: The United States Agriculture Department's top food and nutrition policymaker, under fire from lawmakers who accuse her of mismanaging the department's huge feeding programs, on Wednesday said she would step down next month.
In a resignation letter to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, Undersecretary Ellen Haas said the time had come "to embrace new challenges and use my energies in new ways."

"I am very proud that during my tenure, unprecedented policy and programmatic changes have been achieved in the Department's nutrition mission, reducing hunger and assuring healthier children and a healther nation," she wrote.
A spokeswoman said Haas' departure was effective Feb. 14, and that the undersecretary had no announcements about her next step.

It had been widely expected that Haas would leave with the start of President Clinton's second term although she wanted to stay in office through implementation of the new welfare bill that made signifcant changes in the food stamp program.

Haas had enemies on Capitol Hill who complained she mishandled the transition to healthier school meals. Leaders of the House Agriculture Committee asked last fall for her to be replaced. Even some of Haas' defenders said she sometimes was too assertive in running the nutrition programs and misplayed relations with Congress.

Some opposition among farm state lawmakers and lobbying groups dated from Haas' tenure as head of a consumer group. In that role, she worked for changes in public feeding programs that would reduce fat and other dietary hazards in food.

As undersecretary, Haas oversaw the food stamp program, school lunches, the popular Women and Infants Feeding Program and several other public nutrition programs. Her portfolio accounted for more than 60 percent of USDA spending.

During her four years, Haas achieved two major goals -- reforming the school lunch program so that it complied with the government's dietary guidelines and altering the food stamp program to reduce waste and fraud.
In a statement, Glickman praised Haas.

"Ellen has been a tireless advocate for good nutrition in America, especially for our children. Her drive, determination and energy have never wavered. And in the last four years, the American people have been the beneficiaries," Glickman said.
Haas is the third high level policymaker to resign at the Agriculture Department in the past two months.
